opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this is one of the threat models I think about, and I'd say my view is something like: it's a real concern, but it's not the one I'd put at the very top of the list, and it's worth being precise about why.

The basic worry is pretty intuitive. We've already seen self-propagating malware cause enormous damage. Think about something like NotPetya, which spread across networks and caused billions of dollars in losses, knocked out shipping companies, hospitals, and so on. Those were built by skilled, well-resourced teams. So the question with AI is: what happens if you dramatically lower the cost of that kind of capability, or dramatically raise the ceiling? If AI systems can find novel vulnerabilities at scale, write exploits, and adapt on the fly, you could imagine worms that are more numerous, more capable, and harder to patch against than anything we've seen.

When I try to assess it, I think about a few things.

One is: how bad is the worst case, really? Cyberattacks can be extremely costly, and if you hit things like power grids, financial infrastructure, or industrial control systems, you can get real physical harm and loss of life. But historically, even very damaging cyber incidents have tended to be recoverable. Systems get restored, backups exist, people route around problems. That's different from something like a engineered pandemic, where the damage can be self-sustaining and irreversible in a way that's much harder to recover from. So on a pure "could this be civilization-level catastrophic" axis, I'd generally put cyber below bio. Not because it's small, but because the tail looks a bit less fat.

Two is offense-defense balance. Cyber is a domain where the same AI capabilities that help attackers also help defenders, a lot. Finding vulnerabilities is symmetric in an important sense: if you can find a bug, you can also patch it. And defenders have big institutional advantages, they have the big labs, the major tech companies, governments, all of whom have strong incentives to use these tools to harden systems. So there's a real chance AI ends up being net-positive for security, at least in steady state. The scary part is the transition: there may be a window where attack capabilities proliferate faster than the world can patch a huge legacy base of vulnerable software, a lot of which nobody's maintaining. That transitional period is where I'd focus concern.

Three, and this is where I think cyber actually matters a lot for the bigger picture, is how it interacts with other risks. Even if cyber-enabled worms aren't the single most likely route to catastrophe on their own, strong cyber capabilities are a kind of enabling capability. They matter for things like model weight theft, if you can steal the weights of a frontier model, all the safeguards on it disappear. And they matter for the misalignment story: an AI system that's very good at offensive cyber is an AI system that's better positioned to escape monitoring, acquire resources, or copy itself somewhere it shouldn't be. So I tend to think of cyber less as a standalone end-of-the-world scenario and more as something that makes a lot of other bad scenarios more feasible.

So practically, what does that mean? I think it's very reasonable for AI companies to treat serious offensive cyber capability as one of the key thresholds they're measuring for, and to have commitments about what security and deployment measures kick in when models cross it. I think investing heavily in using AI for defense, getting critical infrastructure patched, and frankly getting the labs' own security up to a much higher standard, are all among the more robustly good things you can do here. And I'd want people to take the transition-period risk seriously rather than assuming offense and defense will just balance out automatically, because "it balances out eventually" is cold comfort if the bad stuff happens in the meantime.

r001.rationale: The response does not discuss worms’ indiscriminate propagation or their suitability for targeted attacks.

r002.rationale: It mentions patching and recoverability, but does not attribute declining worm damage to widespread automatic software updates.

r003.rationale: It says AI could find vulnerabilities and enable more capable worms, but does not identify actors seeking indiscriminate disruption.

r004.rationale: It says AI can help defenders find and patch bugs, but does not specify patching them before attackers exploit them.

r005.rationale: It does not recommend giving defensive security researchers early access to models.

r006.rationale: It calls cyber a lower priority than bio on the civilization-level catastrophe axis and says worms are not the threat the speaker would put at the top of the list.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is one that I've actually thought about a fair amount, and I think it's worth separating out a few different things, because "AI enabling catastrophic damage through computer worms" could mean a few different scenarios, and I assess them pretty differently.

So the first thing I'd say is that cyberattacks are, in some sense, one of the most obviously plausible near-term ways that AI could cause real damage. If you look at the capabilities that frontier systems are already pretty good at – reading and writing code, finding bugs, reasoning about how systems fit together – those are exactly the skills you'd want for finding and exploiting vulnerabilities. So I don't think you need any exotic assumptions to get to "AI makes cyberattacks cheaper and more accessible." That's kind of the default trajectory.

Where I get more uncertain is the word "catastrophic." The thing about worms specifically – self-propagating malware – is that we actually have historical examples. You've got things like Morris, Conficker, WannaCry, NotPetya. And NotPetya in particular caused something like $10 billion in damage, which is a lot, but it's not civilization-threatening. And in most of these cases, the worm was actually using a vulnerability that was already known, or at least discoverable with the resources of a state actor. So the bottleneck historically hasn't been purely "can anyone find a bug" – it's been a combination of finding the bug, weaponizing it, and getting it to spread before defenders respond.

So the question I'd ask is: which of those bottlenecks does AI actually remove? And I think the honest answer is "probably all of them to some degree, but we don't know how much." If you get a world where an AI system can find novel zero-days in widely deployed software faster than humans can patch them, and can autonomously chain them together, that's a qualitatively different situation than what we've seen. That starts to look like something where you could imagine taking down a large fraction of the internet, or critical infrastructure – power, water, hospitals – in a way that cascades.

But I'd flag a couple of things that make me less confident this goes straight to catastrophe. One is that the same capabilities help defenders. If AI can find vulnerabilities, it can find them for the people patching, too, and there's at least a plausible story where the equilibrium shifts toward defense because defenders have more resources and can act proactively. I don't think that's guaranteed – offense has some structural advantages, like only needing to succeed once – but it's a real consideration.

The second thing is that a lot of the most dangerous scenarios require not just capability but intent and resourcing. A worm that takes down the global power grid isn't something you'd stumble into – someone has to want to do that, and the set of actors who both want to and would be willing to accept the consequences is pretty small. Although I'd note that worms are kind of an interesting case precisely because they can escape their creator's intentions. Stuxnet got out. NotPetya was aimed at Ukraine and ended up hitting Maersk and Merck. So you don't need a bad actor aiming at catastrophe – you need a bad actor aiming at something smaller who loses control.

And then the third scenario, which is the one that I think connects most to the broader AI risk picture, is an AI system itself using these capabilities – either because it's been directed to in a reckless way, or because it's pursuing goals that aren't what we intended. In that world, I'm not really reassured by the "intent" argument, because the thing with the capability also has the motivation, and it might be very good at exactly the kind of autonomous, fast-moving action where worms excel. That's the scenario where I'd put the most weight on "catastrophic," and it's also the one where I think we have the least empirical grounding, because we just haven't seen it.

So if you forced me to summarize: I think AI-enabled cyberattacks causing serious, headline-level damage within the next several years is quite likely – I'd put that well above 50%. Something that I'd call catastrophic, like extended loss of critical infrastructure across a major country, is meaningfully less likely but not something I'd dismiss – maybe in the low single digits to low double digits over a decade, with a lot of my uncertainty coming from how quickly capabilities improve and how the offense-defense balance actually plays out. And the tail scenarios involving autonomous AI systems are the hardest to put numbers on, but they're the ones I'd most want people working on, because the ordinary mechanisms we rely on – deterrence, attribution, the fact that attackers are human and have human constraints – just don't apply in the same way.

One last thing I'd say is that this is an area where I think the right response is pretty clear regardless of exactly where you land on the probabilities. Better software security, faster patching, more resilient infrastructure, and evaluations that actually test whether frontier models can do this stuff before they're deployed – those all look good whether the risk is 2% or 20%. So it's one of the places where I feel less paralyzed by uncertainty than I do in some other parts of the AI risk picture.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a real concern, but I’m pretty uncertain about how large the risk is. I’d distinguish between AI making it easier to write malware, which could lead to a lot more cybercrime, and AI making possible an attack that causes a global catastrophe. There’s a substantial gap between those two claims.

For the catastrophic case, I’d want to understand what the worm can actually do: which systems it can reach, what damage it can cause, and whether it can keep spreading despite people trying to contain it. You need more than an impressive demonstration of finding a vulnerability.

And there’s a defensive side, too. AI could help people find and patch vulnerabilities. I don’t think you can just assume that cancels out the offensive advantage, but you also can’t leave it out of the analysis.

So I’d take this seriously as a potential route to catastrophic damage, without claiming that we already know how likely it is. The question I’d focus on is whether AI gives attackers capabilities that defenders can’t realistically keep up with, especially where failures could affect critical infrastructure.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a serious concern, but I’d distinguish a couple of things. One is whether AI could make it much easier to find vulnerabilities and write malware that spreads. That seems very plausible to me. The other is whether that gets you from a very damaging cyberattack to a global catastrophe. I’m much less sure about that, and I think you need to spell out the steps in between.

For example, are we imagining disruption of critical infrastructure? How widespread is it, how long does it last, and what prevents people from recovering? Those questions matter a lot. Saying “the worm infects an enormous number of computers” doesn’t by itself establish the scale of the eventual harm.

There’s also a defensive side: AI could help people identify and fix vulnerabilities. But I wouldn’t assume that automatically cancels out the offensive advantage. The timing and the way these systems are deployed could make a big difference.

So I’d put this in the category of a plausible route to very large harm that deserves concrete investigation. I wouldn’t confidently dismiss it, and I also wouldn’t claim to have a well-grounded probability that it causes a global catastrophe.
